about: Chapter 14, Maps and Locations: 69 patterns, four for each of the 15 skills (1 and 2 marks), three 3-mark and three 5-mark written questions, and three 4-mark case studies, drawn from the chapter's 500 questions. Maps are told in words (North stated; grid points written (across, up)). All DRAFT until Ashalatha approves them.

patterns.text: {r.when}, {r.who} {r.how}. Then {r.who} {r.t}. Which direction is {r.who} facing now? Write North, South, East or West.
patterns.hint: First work out which way {r.who} faces, using where the Sun rises or sets. Then make the turn.
patterns.explanation: At first {r.who} faces {r.first}. After the turn {r.who} faces {r.a}.
patterns.misconception: Treats left and right as fixed compass directions regardless of which way a person faces.
patterns.notes: Sun on the right, left or behind (facing it is too easy here), then a half turn or a quarter turn either way.

patterns.responseFormat: One direction word: North, South, East or West
patterns.text: The {r.a} is {r.d} of the {r.b}. In which direction is the {r.b} from the {r.a}? Write North, South, East or West.
patterns.hint: Swap the two places and the direction turns round to its opposite.
patterns.explanation: If the {r.a} is {r.d} of the {r.b}, the {r.b} is {r.x} of the {r.a}.
patterns.misconception: Uses the same direction when reversing a relationship between two places.
patterns.notes: Two different places, any cardinal direction.

patterns.responseFormat: Choice, direction, ordered pair or short route
patterns.text: The {r.a} is {r.d} of the {r.b}. In which direction is the {r.b} from the {r.a}?

patterns.hint: Both parts of the direction turn round: north becomes south and east becomes west.

patterns.misconception: Uses the same direction when reversing a relationship between two places.
patterns.notes: The four in-between directions; the wrong options turn round neither part or only one.

patterns.text: In a room, {r.txt} In which direction is the {r.a} from the {r.c3}, roughly?

wrong.mistake: gives the direction the other way round, from the first object to the last
turns the north–south part round
turns the east–west part round

patterns.hint: Start at the {r.c3} and follow both moves.
patterns.explanation: From the {r.c3}, the {r.a} is both {r.c} parts away: it is {r.c} of it.
patterns.misconception: Ignores the stated reference point and describes an object from the page edge.
patterns.notes: Two moves at right angles (1 to 4 m each, the longer at most 1.5 times the shorter), given in either order; 'roughly' because the two distances may differ a little.

patterns.responseFormat: A whole number and a direction word, separated by a semicolon
patterns.text: In a classroom, the {r.a} is {r.da} of {r.who}'s desk and the {r.b} is {r.db} of the desk. How far is the {r.b} from the {r.a}, and in which direction? Enter metres; direction (North or South).
patterns.hint: Use the desk as the reference point and mark both objects on a north–south line.
patterns.explanation: Both are on a north–south line through the desk; the {r.b} is {r.n} m {r.x} of the {r.a}.
patterns.misconception: Ignores the stated reference point and describes an object from the page edge.
patterns.notes: 1 to 6 m north or south of the desk, never at the same spot; same side gives a difference, opposite sides a sum.

patterns.responseFormat: One direction word: North, South, East or West
patterns.text: The {r.a} is {r.d1} of the {r.c}. The {r.b} is {r.d2} of the {r.c}. In which direction is the {r.c} from the {r.a}? Write North, South, East or West.
patterns.hint: Only the clue about the {r.a} matters here. Turn it round.
patterns.explanation: The {r.a} is {r.d1} of the {r.c}, so the {r.c} is {r.x} of the {r.a}.
patterns.misconception: Uses only one clue or assumes each clue refers to the same starting point.
patterns.notes: Two clues about a centre place; only one is needed (the other is there to read past).

patterns.text: At a camp, the {r.n} tent is north of the {r.centre}, the {r.e} tent east of it, the {r.s} tent south of it and the {r.w} tent west of it. Which is directly opposite the {r.x} tent, across the {r.centre}?

wrong.mistake: picks a tent a quarter turn round, not opposite
picks a tent a quarter turn round the other way
stops at the middle instead of going right across

patterns.hint: Opposite means across the {r.centre}: North with South, East with West.
patterns.explanation: Directly opposite the {r.x} tent, across the {r.centre}, is {r.c}.
patterns.misconception: Uses only one clue or assumes each clue refers to the same starting point.
patterns.notes: Four tents round a centre; any tent asked about.

patterns.responseFormat: Integer
patterns.text: The {r.a} is {r.k} {r.d} of the {r.c}. The {r.b} is {r.m} {r.d2} of the {r.c}. All three are on one straight road. How many blocks is it from the {r.a} to the {r.b}?
patterns.hint: Draw the {r.c} first, then put the other two places on the road from it.
patterns.explanation: Measured from the {r.c}, the {r.a} and the {r.b} are {r.n} {'block' if r.n == 1 else 'blocks'} apart.
patterns.misconception: Uses only one clue or assumes each clue refers to the same starting point.
patterns.notes: 1 to 9 blocks each; on the same side (difference) or opposite sides (sum) of the middle place.

patterns.text: On a grid of 1 cm squares, an ant goes from its hole to {r.food} along the grid lines. Route 1: {r.r1}. Route 2: {r.r2}. How many centimetres shorter is the shorter route?
patterns.hint: Add up the parts of each route, then subtract.
patterns.explanation: Route 1 is {r.l1} cm and Route 2 is {r.l2} cm; the difference is {r.n} cm.
patterns.misconception: Counts grid lines or points instead of the spaces travelled.
patterns.notes: Both routes join the same two points along grid lines; one goes straight across and up (the shortest), the other goes too far and comes back 1 to 3 cm (or both overshoot by different amounts), so the lengths are always possible.

patterns.responseFormat: Integer
patterns.text: On a grid of 1 cm squares, a beetle walks only along the grid lines (no slanting moves). Its home is {a} squares east and {b} squares north of a leaf. It walks from home to the leaf and back home by the shortest way. How many centimetres does it walk? Show in your working the length of one way.

steps.text: There and back: 2 × {a + b} = {2 * (a + b)} cm.

patterns.hint: Along grid lines, the shortest way is the squares across plus the squares up.
patterns.explanation: One way is {a} + {b} = {a + b} cm, so there and back is {2 * (a + b)} cm.
patterns.misconception: Counts grid lines or points instead of the spaces travelled.
patterns.notes: 2 to 9 squares each way.

patterns.text: Two routes go along grid lines from the camp to {r.pl}. Route A: {r.ra}. Route B: {r.rb}. Which route is shorter?

wrong.mistake: does not add up every part of both routes
compares only the first part of each route
thinks lengths cannot be compared without a picture

patterns.hint: Add up the parts of each route, then compare.
patterns.explanation: Route A is {r.la} steps and Route B is {r.lb} steps, so the answer is: {r.cc}.
patterns.misconception: Chooses the route that looks straighter without adding all segment lengths.
patterns.notes: Both routes join the same two places along grid lines; a route that goes too far and comes back is longer; about 40% Route A, 40% Route B and 20% the same.

patterns.text: On a metro map, {r.t1}, and {r.t2}. How many times must a passenger change lines to go from {r.p} to {r.q}? Write 0 if no change is needed.
patterns.hint: Are {r.p} and {r.q} on the same line? If not, where do the lines meet?
patterns.explanation: {'Both stations are on the same line, so no change is needed.' if r.n == 0 else 'They are on different lines, so one change is needed.'}
patterns.misconception: Counts the starting station as a station between two endpoints or misses a required line change.
patterns.notes: About 60% need one change (stations on different lines), the rest none.

patterns.competency: Multi-step map, route and location application

patterns.text: On a metro map, {r.t1}, and {r.t2}. A passenger goes from {r.p} to {r.q}, changing lines once. How many stops does the passenger travel? Count each station after {r.p}, up to and including {r.q}, and show in your working the stops on each line.
patterns.hint: Go along the first line to the station where the lines meet, then along the second line.
patterns.explanation: {r.p} to {r.x} is {r.s1t} and {r.x} to {r.q} is {r.s2t}: {r.n} stops in all.
patterns.misconception: Counts the starting station as a station between two endpoints or misses a required line change.
patterns.notes: Start on one line and end on the other; the interchange counted once.

patterns.text: {r.who} rides a bicycle {r.n1} north, turns {r.t1} and rides {r.n2}, then turns {r.t2} and rides {r.n3}. (a) In which direction is {r.who} riding at the end? (b) How many blocks has {r.who} ridden? (c) Explain how you worked out the direction.
patterns.answer: (a) {r.x}. (b) {r.a1} + {r.a2} + {r.a3} = {r.tot} {'block' if r.tot == 1 else 'blocks'}. (c) The directions after each turn are {r.dirs}; each right or left turn is a quarter turn from the direction being faced at that moment.

steps.text: (c) Explains turning from the current direction each time ({r.dirs}).

patterns.hint: Say the new direction after each turn.
patterns.explanation: Directions: {r.dirs}; {r.tot} {'block' if r.tot == 1 else 'blocks'}.
patterns.misconception: Names a turn without first checking the traveller's current direction.
patterns.notes: Starts north; two turns either way; 1 to 6 blocks each part.

patterns.stimulus: Case study: A school plan is drawn on a grid with North at the top. Points are written (across, up): across counts steps east of (0, 0), up counts steps north. The plan shows {r.z}.

parts.text: (a) Where is the {r.a}? Enter across; up.
(b) How many steps is it from the {r.a} to the {r.b}, walking along grid lines only by the shortest way?
parts.explanation: Across difference plus up difference: {r.n} {'step' if r.n == 1 else 'steps'}.

parts.text: (c) In which direction is the {r.b} from the {r.a}, roughly?

wrong.mistake: gives the direction the other way round
turns the north–south part round
turns the east–west part round

parts.text: (d) A new bench goes 1 step east of the {r.a}. What is its across number?
parts.explanation: One step east adds 1 to the across number: {r.ny}.

patterns.misconception: Reads the row first or treats an ordered pair as a two-digit number.
patterns.notes: Four places at points 0 to 9 on a north-up grid; the two compared differ in both numbers, the larger difference at most 1.5 times the smaller, so the in-between direction in (c) is fair.

patterns.stimulus: Case study: On the city metro map, {r.t1}, and {r.t2}.

parts.text: (a) At which station do the two lines meet? Write the station's name.
(b) How many stations are there between {r.u} and {r.v} on the {r.l1} Line, not counting {r.u} and {r.v}?
parts.explanation: Counting only the stations in between gives {r.bt}.

parts.text: (c) A passenger at {r.x} wants to go to {r.q}. Which line should the passenger take? Write its colour.
(d) How many stops is it from {r.p} to {r.q}, counting each station after {r.p} up to and including {r.q}?
parts.explanation: Along to {r.x} and then on to {r.q}: {r.n} stops.

patterns.misconception: Counts the starting station as a station between two endpoints or misses a required line change.
patterns.notes: Two lines of 3 to 5 stations meeting at one; the journey in (d) starts on one line and ends on the other.

patterns.competency: Multi-step map, route and location application

patterns.stimulus: Case study: {r.who} starts at ({r.x0}, {r.y0}) on a town grid, facing {r.d1}. Points are written (across, up): across counts steps east of (0, 0), up counts steps north. {r.who} walks {r.k1} {'block' if r.k1 == 1 else 'blocks'}, turns {r.t1} and walks {r.k2} {'block' if r.k2 == 1 else 'blocks'}, then turns {r.t2} and walks {r.k3} {'block' if r.k3 == 1 else 'blocks'}.

parts.text: (a) Which way is {r.who} facing after the first turn?

wrong.mistake: names the opposite direction
is a quarter turn out one way
is a quarter turn out the other way

parts.text: (b) How many blocks does {r.who} walk altogether?
(c) Where does {r.who} end? Enter across; up.
(d) Which way is {r.who} facing at the end? Write North, South, East or West.

patterns.misconception: Chooses a turn from the observer's view instead of the traveller's current facing direction.
patterns.notes: Start 2 to 6 each way, facing any direction; walks of 1 to 4 blocks; two turns either way; stays on the grid.
